analysis.one_liner: Narrows which streams and wetlands get federal Clean Water Act pollution protection.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote; it never reached the Senate floor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the Clean Water Act's definition of federally protected waters. It would keep federal protection for territorial seas, interstate waters used for commerce, permanent streams and rivers that flow into them, and adjacent wetlands with a visible surface connection. It would strip federal protection from streams that flow only after rain or snowmelt, groundwater, most ditches and drainage systems, and wetlands without a continuous surface connection, and it would create a fast, government-paid process for landowners to get a binding ruling that waters on their property are not protected.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers, real estate developers, and mining or energy companies that build on or discharge into currently protected waters. They would face fewer federal permits and less liability for filling streams, draining wetlands, and releasing pollution into waters the bill removes from federal jurisdiction. Landowners would also gain a binding, free, 60-day federal determination that waters on their land are unprotected, enforceable in court.

how_it_helps.text: The bill excludes intermittent and ephemeral waters — streams that flow only in response to rain or snowmelt — from federal Clean Water Act jurisdiction [S3].

It also excludes groundwater, including water drained through subsurface drainage systems like drain tiling, man-made ditches, prior converted cropland, irrigation areas, artificial ponds, stormwater controls, and waste treatment systems [S3].
Wetlands are protected only if they are adjacent to and have a continuous surface water connection that an ordinary person could see with the naked eye [S3].

It creates a new process where landowners and permit applicants can request a binding federal determination of whether waters on their property are covered, made at government cost within 60 days, with the property deemed unprotected if the agency misses the deadline, and with expedited court review available [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People downstream. Many drinking water supplies and beloved fishing and swimming waters are fed by streams that flow seasonally, and wetlands without a visible surface connection still filter pollution and absorb floods. If those waters lose federal protection, pollution discharged upstream flows into the waters that remain protected, and taxpayers and water ratepayers bear more of the cost of cleaning it up.

drawbacks.text: Removing federal protection from seasonal streams and disconnected wetlands allows pollution discharged into them to reach larger protected waters downstream, weakening the pollution controls the Clean Water Act was meant to provide [S3].

The bill requires that jurisdictional questions be resolvable by naked-eye visual inspection, excluding any water that needs aerial photos, satellite imaging, or hydrological testing to classify, which is a difficulty of proving coverage rather than a fact about the water [S3].

Supporters argue the current rules reach too far and burden private landowners with unclear federal permit requirements; the bill answers that by defining covered waters narrowly and giving landowners a binding, government-funded determination on request [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives landowners and developers real regulatory certainty and a fast, free ruling process, which are genuine benefits. The cost falls diffusely on everyone downstream: seasonal streams and isolated-feeling wetlands feed the rivers and aquifers people drink from, fish in, and use for recreation, and once they are open to discharges and filling, that pollution moves downstream. The bill resolves landowner uncertainty by shrinking the protected resource rather than by clarifying how it is regulated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken on it.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Braun introduced the bill on June 22, 2021, with Sens. Joni Ernst and Chuck Grassley as cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day [S1][S5].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died there when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Seasonal streams and wetlands keep the federal protection they had, so the people who benefit are downstream water users and everyone who relies on the existing Clean Water Act rules; the landowners and industries the bill would have relieved from federal permitting did not get that relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Downstream water users and existing Clean Water Act rules

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored it, and with Democrats controlling the Senate, it never advanced past committee.

industries.note: The bill would exclude drain tiling, prior converted cropland, irrigation systems, and drainage ditches from federal jurisdiction, relieving farm operations of Clean Water Act permitting. The runoff those systems channel into seasonal streams ends up in downstream waters the public uses.

Developers could fill seasonal streams and wetlands without a visible surface connection without a federal permit, and could obtain a binding, government-funded determination within 60 days that waters on a site are unprotected. That lowers construction costs but removes protections from the wetlands and streams that absorb floods and filter water.

industries.industry: Mining, oil and gas, and other heavy industry
industries.note: Discharges into seasonal streams and construction in water-filled depressions incidental to mining would fall outside federal jurisdiction. Pollution released into those waters flows into rivers that remain federally protected.

industries.industry: Water utilities and downstream water users
industries.note: With more upstream waters open to discharges, utilities and the communities they serve face dirtier source water and higher treatment costs.
